builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
summary: The technique replaces trusting an agent's self-reported success or answer-only LLM grading with trajectory-level LLM judging augmented by a rule-based checker grounded in the actual environment state (here, EHR responses). The cost is additional inference per evaluated trajectory, engineering of domain-specific rules, and the need to expose full tool outputs to the judge; including the agent's reasoning adds tokens without improving detection and degrades detection of misreported values by 0.18. It can fail on errors that leave the final answer unchanged, on incorrectly reported clinical values (the hardest category, missed even with reasoning traces), and on domain-model judges that miss dangerous cases such as medication overdoses, so judges alone cannot be the safety boundary.
rationale: The reader can run open-weight LLM judges plus rule-based checks on a single GPU or via APIs to validate agent outputs, but the 0.75 discrimination ceiling and category-specific blind spots require validation on the reader's own workload before production reliance.

claims.statement: The technique replaces trusting an agent's self-reported success or answer-only LLM grading with trajectory-level LLM judging augmented by a rule-based checker grounded in the actual environment state (here, EHR responses). The cost is additional inference per evaluated trajectory, engineering of domain-specific rules, and the need to expose full tool outputs to the judge; including the agent's reasoning adds tokens without improving detection and degrades detection of misreported values by 0.18. It can fail on errors that leave the final answer unchanged, on incorrectly reported clinical values (the hardest category, missed even with reasoning traces), and on domain-model judges that miss dangerous cases such as medication overdoses, so judges alone cannot be the safety boundary.

With full trajectory information, judge discrimination between unsafe and correct actions reaches 0.75; access to actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39, and combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker detects 97% of injected faults, while answer-only judging flags 56% of correct trajectories as unsafe.
